subject: Coding
topic: How the event loop decides what runs next

scenes.myth: JavaScript executes asynchronous callbacks in the order they are scheduled.
scenes.fact: Microtasks like Promises jump ahead of Macrotasks like setTimeout every single time.
scenes.sayMyth: Your Promise logged before your timer and broke your code.
scenes.sayFact: The event loop is the engine's traffic controller that decides whether your code or the browser's UI updates get to run next.

nodes.label: Call Stack
nodes.say: When code runs on the Call Stack, synchronous execution takes full control.

nodes.label: Microtask Queue
nodes.say: Before taking any new task, the loop drains the Microtask Queue where Promises wait.

nodes.label: Macrotask Queue
nodes.say: Only after microtasks are empty does the loop check the Macrotask Queue for timers.

scenes.title: Queue Execution Hierarchy

left.title: Microtasks
left.say: Microtasks — like promise resolutions — run immediately when the current code finishes.

right.title: Macrotasks
right.say: Macrotasks — like timers and click events — wait in line behind every microtask.

scenes.sayVerdict: The event loop drains every single microtask before running the next macrotask.

steps.say: As recursive promises clog the microtask queue, the browser tries to render the next frame.
At the 16 millisecond mark, the UI frame paint is blocked because microtasks never yield.
The loading spinner freezes completely as microtasks stack up and monopolize the main thread.

scenes.narration: If you need to process 10,000 items without dropping frames, do you chain Promises or use setTimeout?
scenes.text: If you need to process 10,000 items without dropping frames, do you chain Promises or use setTimeout? One will kill your UI, the other lets the browser breathe.
scenes.hint: Think about which queue yields back to screen painting.

meta.title: JavaScript Event Loop: How Priority Actually Works #Shorts
meta.description:
Understand how the JavaScript event loop manages task priority. We bust the myth that asynchronous callbacks run in the order they are scheduled by comparing microtasks and macrotasks.

Learn why recursive promise chains can block browser repaints.
See how setTimeout lets the browser breathe during heavy tasks.
Discover which method prevents UI freezes when processing 10,000 items.

Which strategy would you use to process 10,000 items without dropping frames?

Mastering the event loop is essential for writing high-performance web applications, understanding asynchronous programming, and debugging common browser rendering issues.
